newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn ready to delay gold plan, Tietmeyer sees deal.
newsitem.headline: Bonn ready to delay gold plan, Tietmeyer sees deal.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition backed down on Tuesday on a controversial plan to revalue central bank assets after parliamentary deputies from Kohl's party sharply criticised the proposal.
A source in the ruling coalition said protests from conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) deputies forced the coalition to retreat from the plan to revalue central bank reserves.
"A solution is only possible with support of the Bundesbank," the coalition source told Reuters. "In face of the resistance from the Bundesbank, the revaluation for 1997 is no longer on the table."

Abandoning the plan to revalue the assets will mean that there is another 10 billion mark ($5.8 billion) hole in the 1997 budget, the official said. To fill that hole, the coalition was discussing privatisations, budget cuts and moderate tax increases.
Earlier, Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said they were on the way to coming to an agreement on revaluing gold and currency reserves.

Waigel and Tietmeyer spoke briefly to journalists after a meeting at the Finance Ministry in Bonn. Despite attempts to keep the meeting secret, dozens of journalists were on hand as Waigel and Tietmeyer concluded their meeting.
"We had good talks and we are on the way to an agreement," Waigel said.
"We are indeed," Tietmeyer added. "I hope that we can come to an agreement."
They declined to provide further details and walked quickly away.

There had been considerable speculation that the two would meet to search for ways to resolve the extraordinary public dispute between the central bank and the government over Waigel's plans to revalue Bundesbank gold and currency assets this year.
Michael Glos, head of the Christian Social Union (CSU) parliamentary group, said that the differences between the Bundesbank and the government had been too small to fight over.
"We are not far apart on this," Glos said. "A public dispute is not worth it either for the Bundesbank or for the government. We have a saying -- the smarter one backs down."
The Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold in its reserves, valued at 13.7 billion marks ($8 billion) compared to a current market value of more than 55 billion marks.

The central bank said it was not in principle opposed to revaluing its gold reserves but insisted that the process should not take place until 1999, or at least not before the decision as to who will participate in monetary union, in May 1998. ($ = 1.727 German Marks)
